questions.text: A restaurant chef requests food prep counter heights of 950 mm to accommodate taller staff. According to ergonomic standards, how should the designer respond?

options.text: Approve 950 mm; higher counters are always more efficient, although this may not be true for all tasks and user heights
Reject; standard counter height is 850–900 mm for optimal ergonomics and Philippine anthropometric data.
Approve; heights above 900 mm improve workflow, but this depends on specific tasks and user preferences
Use variable heights: 950 mm for tall staff, 800 mm for others, to accommodate a wider range of user heights and tasks

rationale.a: 950 mm exceeds standard and may create strain for average-height staff.
rationale.c: Non-standard heights (950+ mm) conflict with equipment integration and reduce efficiency.
rationale.d: Variable heights complicate equipment installation and violate design standards.
rationale.correct: Food prep counters are standardized at 850–900 mm height per ergonomic and code standards. This accounts for optimal arm height during extended standing work and reduces fatigue.
rationale.takeaway: Food prep counter height = 850–900 mm. This is ergonomic standard, not negotiable by individual preference.

questions.text: A restaurant dining area serves 320 patrons and is unsprinklered. According to RA 9514 2019 IRR Section 10.2, what is the minimum total exit width required?

rationale.a: ERR-DSGN-019: Using 5 mm/person is substandard and creates fire safety hazard.
rationale.c: 10 mm/person exceeds code; 7.6 mm is the standard.
rationale.d: 900 mm is accessible door minimum, not exit width calculation for large occupancies.
rationale.correct: Exit width = occupancy × 7.6 mm/person per PD 1096 §906. 320 × 7.6 = 2432 mm (2.432 m).
rationale.takeaway: Exit width formula: occupants × 7.6 mm/person. For 320 people = 2432 mm minimum.

questions.text: A restaurant has 600 sqm total floor area dedicated to dining. According to standard kitchen design practice, what is the minimum required kitchen floor area?

rationale.a: ERR-DSGN-031: 1:4 ratio (150 sqm) undersizes the kitchen and violates code. Correct ratio is 1:3.
rationale.c: 1:2 ratio oversizes the kitchen beyond necessary; 1:3 is the standard.
rationale.d: 1:1 ratio (600 sqm kitchen) is operationally inefficient and violates space efficiency standards.
rationale.correct: Kitchen-to-dining ratio = 1:3 per standard restaurant design practice. 600 sqm dining ÷ 3 = 200 sqm kitchen minimum.
rationale.takeaway: Kitchen:dining = 1:3. For 600 sqm dining, kitchen = 200 sqm. Common trap: reversing the ratio.

questions.text: Per local zoning ordinance (not PD 1096), how many parking spaces are required for a restaurant with 450 sqm of dining area?

rationale.a: 9 spaces (1/50 sqm) is insufficient; restaurant standard is 1/30 sqm.
rationale.c: 30 spaces exceeds requirement (that would be 1/15 sqm ratio).
rationale.d: 45 spaces is excessive (1/10 sqm is not a code threshold).
rationale.correct: Restaurant parking = 1 space per 30 sqm of dining area per PD 1096 §803. 450 ÷ 30 = 15 spaces.
rationale.takeaway: Restaurant parking formula: Dining area ÷ 30 sqm/space. Distinguish from hotel (1/room) and hospital (1/4 beds).

questions.text: A restaurant design proposal allocates 300 sqm to dining and 300 sqm to kitchen within a 600 sqm total building. When reviewing this allocation, what design issue arises under standard restaurant practice?

options.text: Kitchen is correctly sized at 1:1 ratio; no issue, as this allows for equal space distribution
ERR-DSGN-031: Kitchen oversized; standard 1:3 ratio requires kitchen = 100 sqm for 300 sqm dining.
Dining oversized; should increase kitchen to 450 sqm, which would provide more space for kitchen operations
Allocation is acceptable if parking exceeds 20 spaces, which may offset the space distribution concerns

rationale.a: 1:1 ratio violates standard practice; kitchen should be ONE-THIRD of dining area, not equal.
rationale.c: Dining is correctly sized; reducing kitchen from 300 to 100 sqm is the appropriate correction.
rationale.d: Parking requirement is independent of dining/kitchen ratio efficiency.
rationale.correct: For 300 sqm dining, kitchen should be 100 sqm (1:3 ratio), not 300 sqm. The 300 sqm kitchen oversizes operational space, reduces floor efficiency, and increases utility costs.
rationale.takeaway: ERR-DSGN-031 trap: Kitchen:dining = 1:3. A 300 sqm kitchen for 300 sqm dining is 3× oversized.

questions.text: A restaurant has 200 dining seats. According to RA 9514, what is the minimum dining floor area required?

rationale.a: 200 sqm equals seat count but ignores the 1.4 sqm/seat requirement.
rationale.c: 286 sqm is close but results from incorrect calculation (e.g., 1.43 sqm/seat).
rationale.d: 400 sqm exceeds requirement; 280 sqm is the minimum.
rationale.correct: No minimum dining floor area requirement from RA 9514; 1.4 sqm/seat is for occupant load/egress calculation only per RA 9514 IRR Table 10.
rationale.takeaway: Dining occupant load = seats × 1.4 sqm/seat. This is the code standard under RA 9514.

questions.text: What occupancy group classification applies to a restaurant under PD 1096?

options.text: Group C (Education/Recreation), which is typically reserved for educational facilities and recreational centers
Group H (Assembly), which includes spaces designed for gatherings of people for purposes such as dining, entertainment, or worship
Group D (Institutional), generally applicable to facilities like hospitals and care homes

rationale.a: Group C applies to schools and churches. Restaurants are NOT educational institutions.
rationale.c: ERR-DSGN-005: Group H is for large assembly venues (stadiums, arenas). Restaurants are not classified as pure assembly.
rationale.d: Group D is institutional (hospitals, jails). Restaurants do not provide custodial care.
rationale.correct: Restaurants are classified as Group E (business and mercantile) per PD 1096. Dining areas and food service operations fall under commercial occupancies.
rationale.takeaway: Restaurant = Group E occupancy, not C or H. This is a foundational classification error trap.

questions.text: A restaurant kitchen requires two main aisles for equipment access and service. According to standard practice, what is the minimum width for a kitchen aisle?

rationale.a: 0.9 m is too narrow for equipment movement and violates work zone safety.
rationale.b: 1.0 m is insufficient; 1.2 m is the recognized standard.
rationale.d: 1.5 m exceeds standard requirement but may be used for high-volume kitchens.
rationale.correct: Kitchen aisle minimum width = 1.2 m per standard restaurant design practice. This accommodates equipment movement and two-way service traffic.
rationale.takeaway: Kitchen aisle minimum = 1.2 m. Remember this distinct from 900 mm door width and 1.5 m pathway standards.

questions.text: A restaurant design uses a single emergency exit serving 75 dining patrons. According to PD 1096 Section 906, is this design compliant?

options.text: Yes, single exit is permitted for up to 150 persons.
No, dual exits are required at 50+ person occupancy.
Yes, single exit is permitted if width exceeds 1200 mm.
No, restaurants always require minimum three exits.

rationale.a: Incorrect threshold. Dual exits required at 50+, not 150+.
rationale.c: Exit width calculation does not substitute for dual exit requirement.
rationale.d: Three exits not required for 75 occupants; two exits minimum suffice.
rationale.correct: ERR-DSGN-021 violation: PD 1096 §906 requires dual exits at occupancies of 50 or more persons. Single exit at 75 occupants fails fire code.
rationale.takeaway: Occupancy threshold = 50 persons. At 50+ = 2 exits required minimum. Single exit fails at 75 occupants.

questions.text: A restaurant kitchen has food prep areas adjacent to the dishwashing section with only a low counter separating them. According to DOH/FSDO regulation, what design violation exists?

options.text: No violation; proximity allows efficient workflow, assuming all hygiene standards are met
Violation: Dishwashing must be physically separated from raw food prep to prevent cross-contamination.
Violation exists only if prep counter is below 850 mm height, which is not a standard regulation
No violation if aisle width meets 1.2 m minimum, which is unrelated to cross-contamination concerns

rationale.a: Workflow efficiency does not override food safety requirements. Separation is mandatory.
rationale.c: Counter height is about ergonomics; separation is about sanitation compliance.
rationale.d: Aisle width is about circulation; it does not substitute for sanitation zone separation.
rationale.correct: DOH/FSDO food safety standards require physical separation (walls, sealed barriers) between dishwashing and raw food preparation zones to prevent cross-contamination and pathogen spread.
rationale.takeaway: Dishwashing isolated from raw prep: DOH/FSDO requirement. Low counters do NOT satisfy separation mandate.
